t: Tlingit society is divided into two moieties, the Raven and the Eagle, made up of clans in which descent and inheritance pass through the mother's line.
The 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic killed about 60% of the Mainland Tlingit and 37% of the Island Tlingit.
Tribes, institutions and linguists are working to revitalize the Tlingit language, which has an estimated 200 to 400 speakers in the United States and 100 in Canada.
dyk: The name Lingít means 'People of the Tides', while the old Russian name for them, Koloshi, came from a Sugpiaq-Alutiiq word for the labret worn by women.
ev: Human culture with elements related to the Tlingit arises near the mouths of the Skeena and Nass Rivers
The Tlingit first meet Europeans, Russian explorers
Yeilxaak, the first chief of Klukwan encountered by Europeans, dies
The Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic kills about 60% of the Mainland Tlingit
Many Tlingit convert to Orthodox Christianity as their shamans cannot treat Old World diseases

f.homeland: Lingít Aaní, the Land of the Tlingit: from Yakutat south through the Alaskan Panhandle and the Alexander Archipelago, and inland along the Alsek, Tatshenshini, Chilkat, Taku and Stikine rivers to Atlin, Teslin and Tagish Lakes in northwestern British Columbia and the southern Yukon
f.period: Human culture with elements related to the Tlingit from around 10,000 years ago; first contact with Russian explorers in 1741 and Spanish in 1775; the 1862 smallpox epidemic; conversions to Orthodox Christianity between 1886 and 1895; today federally recognized tribes in Alaska and First Nations in Canada
f.known: matrilineal clans within the Raven and Eagle moieties; heraldic crests on totem poles, canoes and house posts; cedar plank clan houses; at.oow, inherited objects held in trust; a rich oratory tradition; Chilkat and Ravenstail weaving; salmon fisheries
f.sources: The Tlingit's own traditions and present-day communities; Russian sources such as Grigory Shelikhov's 1796 map; ethnographies such as those by Frederica de Laguna, George Thornton Emmons and Sergei Kan; Swanton's Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); genetic studies of HLA genes
